### III.5 Detector & Readout Electronics

*Figure 16: The EXCITE detector enclosure. The detector itself is mounted inside the black box. The two short baffle tubes allow light from each spectrometer channel to individually reach the detector. Short pass filters in the baffle tubes limit the thermal background incident on the detector. Photo taken by Sophia Roberts/NASA.*

The EXCITE infrared detector is a Teledyne HgCdTe Astronomy Wide Area Infrared Imager with 2k resolution, reference pixels, and guide mode operation (H2RG). [36] The detector used by EXCITE during its test flight was an engineering unit left over from JWST/NIRSpec development. For the LDB science flight, EXCITE will use a NIRSpec flight candidate H2RG whose performance is summarized by Rauscher et al. [52]. The detector is sensitive between 0.8–5.3 µm. For operating temperatures below $\sim$ 65 K, the detector’s dark current noise contribution to EXCITE’s error budget is negligible. [53] Compared to other NIR detector technologies (e.g., InSb), HgCdTe detectors achieve lower dark current at higher temperatures, matching EXCITE’s cryogenic solution. The H2RG is located in a blackened box that has two apertures to allow incident light to shine from each of the spectrograph channels. These apertures, located at the end of short baffle tubes, contain short-pass filters with a cutoff wavelength of 3.5 µm. The filters block unwanted thermal emission from the optics, and the baffle configuration limits stray light from the spectrograph. A photo of the EXCITE detector enclosure is shown in Figure 16. The detector has four output channels, each corresponding to a 2048 $\times$ 512 pixel quadrant of the detector. The spectra land on channels 1 and 4. Channels 2 and 3 sample stray light. The maximum flux per pixel on the H2RG for a bright target is 5863 e-/s in CH1 and 1283 e-/s in CH2, corresponding to saturation times of about 20.5 s and 93.5 s, respectively.

The detector is read out using an ACADIA controller. [37] The ACADIA was developed for the Roman Space Telescope (RST). The ACADIA is maintained at a stable temperature near 130 K. The intended detector readout scheme is described by Nagler et al. [44] and is further detailed in Section IV of this paper. The ACADIA and H2RG are read out by a Multi-purpose ASIC Control and Interface Electronics (MACIE) controller card. The MACIE is designed to read out Teledyne HxRGs. The MACIE operates at ambient temperature and is installed inside the Detector Control Box (DCB), located on the underside of the gondola’s inner frame.

The EXCITE science detector was extensively characterized by the NIRSpec team, with performance and operation verified by EXCITE. Custom firmware was developed to interface the ACADIA with EXCITE’s detectors. It has been validated in both laboratory and flight settings. Assuming that we will read two windows of 512 $\times$ 248 pixels (see Section IV), the detector system’s data rate is 350 MB per hour in flight. A 60-day flight would result in just over 500 GB of detector data.

## IV Simulation Tools, Data Reduction, & Systematics

We have developed simulation tools to quantify EXCITE’s expected sensitivity and evaluate the impact of systematic effects we expect to encounter with EXCITE. These include both correlated and uncorrelated effects. Building upon work by Nagler et al., [45] we show that we expect EXCITE to be background-limited across its entire band. We have also quantified noise due to pointing jitter, evaluating the impact of both absolute pointing errors (APE) and random pointing errors (RPE). We find that noise due to jitter is subdominant to radiometric noise. We have also generated time series of simulated focal plane images that contain full-orbit phase curves of hot Jupiters.

To generate the time series spectral images and perform radiometric calculations, we use the ExoSim2 simulator. [43, 42, 41] ExoSim2 is a highly-configurable time domain end-to-end simulator that also provides radiometric signal and noise estimates for instruments intended to perform point source photometry and spectroscopy. ExoSim2 can generate spectral images that may include photon noise, pointing jitter, detector dark current, read noise, and more. We use the dynamic capabilities of ExoSim2 to create stacks of spectral images and inject the exoplanet signal as well as balloon systematics in order to perform statistical detrending of the phase curve amplitude. [55] Section IV.1 describes the methods used to calculate noise from uncorrelated sources and shows a radiometric model for EXCITE. Section IV.2 details the expected noise contributions due to jitter and reports a total noise budget for EXCITE. Section IV.3 describes the front-end data reduction pipeline that we plan to use during flight in order to monitor data quality at the detector stage and assess real-time instrument performance.

### IV.1 Uncorrelated Noise

To quantify the photon noise from uncorrelated sources, we calculate the photon signal from the target star, the Zodiacal background, the foreground emission from the Earth’s atmosphere, and the thermal emission from the instrument. Photon signals are assumed to obey Poisson statistics. We account for the total optical efficiency of the instrument using measured and/or calculated values of each optical element’s transmission or reflection spectrum, and we account for the detector’s quantum efficiency using data presented by Rauscher et al. [52] The total throughput of the EXCITE optical system is shown in Figure 17. Once the total throughput and photon signals are calculated, ExoSim2 uses an empirically found wavelength solution for the EXCITE optical system and estimates synthetic apertures for each spectral bin, where we set the encircled energy to be 91%. The radiometric output of the simulator is a table containing signals and noises in units ct/s per spectral bin.

### IV.2 Pointing Jitter

Pointing jitter along the telescope boresight is another source of noise. It leads to variable losses at the field stop and signal modulation at the science focal plane. We treat these two situations separately. We show that even in the absence of advanced detrending techniques, noise due to jitter is always subdominant to photon noise. In principle, the spectral image gives a precise measurement of the line-of-sight, and if the throughput loss as a function of line-of-sight variations at the field stop is known, then the noise induced by jitter can be completely detrended. Recent work by Bocchieri et al. [12] outlines a method for detrending jitter from spectral images generated by ExoSim2. They find that, even in the case when $N_{\text{jitter}}$ is much less than other sources of photon noise, properly detrending jitter significantly decreases the bias of statistically retrieved transit depths.

To estimate the noise associated with pointing jitter at the field stop ( $N_{\text{field stop}}$ ), we first calculate the EXCITE PSF using a 2D Fourier transform of the as-built telescope aperture. We then calculate the width of the field stop in the image plane for each wavelength and generate an RPE timestream that moves the image of the field stop on the PSF. EXCITE uses a rectangular field stop with a width of 100 µm; the plate scale of the optical system at the field stop is 34.4 mas/µm. At each time step, we integrate the flux, $F$ , of the PSF inside the field stop. The resulting noise is calculated as $N_{\text{field stop}}=\text{std}(F)/\bar{F}$ over the entire timestream, where $\text{std}(F)$ is the standard deviation of the flux and $\bar{F}$ is the average flux. We can vary the APE (offsets from the beam center to the field stop), RPE, and integration time. Based on the pointing results from the 2023 SuperBIT flight,[24] we created our timestreams with a 1- $\sigma$ RPE of 50 mas at 1 Hz, APE of 100 mas, and 2 hr integration times. We find that $N_{\text{field stop}}<25$ ppm across 0.8–3.5 µm. $N_{\text{field stop}}$ peaks at around 2.3 µm. At this wavelength, the field stop starts to vignette the first sidelobe of the PSF. Similarly, the jitter noise is relatively large at 0.8 µm and 3.4 µm due to vignetting of the second sidelobe and the main lobe, respectively.

To simulate noise due to jitter at the science focal plane ( $N_{\text{focal plane}}$ ), we centered an Airy profile with diameter $D(\lambda)$ on a grid of detector pixels where the QE of each pixel was only known to $\pm$ 0.1% at 1- $\sigma$ . Using a plate scale of 12.8 mas/µm at the focal plane, we created another jitter timestream with 1- $\sigma$ RPE of 50 mas at 1 Hz. At each point in time, we jittered the PSF location and integrated the flux of the PSF multiplied by a random QE map with the assumed uncertainty. We used rectangular apertures that have widths of the nearest integer number of pixels such that $\sim$ $2.5D(\lambda)$ were captured, or about $91\%$ of the encircled energy of the PSF. The apertures were centered on the middle of the grid and remained static through time since 50 mas corresponds to a linear translation of about one-fifth the size of a pixel on the focal plane. The resulting noise $N_{\text{focal plane}}$ is calculated in the same way as $N_{\text{field stop}}$ . We find that $N_{\text{focal plane}}<24$ ppm at 2 hr integration times. $N_{\text{focal plane}}$ peaks at 0.8 µm where the PSF is concentrated on the fewest number of pixels. It decreases like $1/\lambda$ out to 3.5 µm. The total noise due to jitter is given by $N_{\text{jitter}}=\sqrt{N_{\text{field stop}}^{2}+N_{\text{focal plane}}^{2}}$ and is shown in Figure 19. The calculated jitter noise is subdominant across the EXCITE band.

Figure 19 shows the sensitivity in ppm for EXCITE when combining radiometric sources and pointing jitter. We show the contributions to the total sensitivity from the target star, pointing jitter, and other radiometric sources, i.e., the Earth’s atmosphere and instrument emission. The sensitivity profiles are plotted as $N/S_{\star}$ , where $N$ is the noise from a source or a combination of sources, and $S_{\star}$ is the signal from the target star. The results are scaled to integration times of 2 hr, which is about the duration of the secondary eclipse for many of EXCITE’s candidate targets. The secondary eclipse depths are calculated using Equation 1.

### IV.3 Simulated Spectral Images & Line-of-Sight Pipeline

When the payload is launched from the Antarctic, there will be a period of time when we maintain line-of-sight contact with the instrument, enabling high-rate telemetry. During this period we will tune the instrument for the float environment and verify that the instrument is performing nominally at the beginning of the flight. We call this the “line-of-sight” portion of the flight. The EXCITE Line-of-sight Diagnostic Pipeline (ELDiP) is a data reduction pipeline with multiple diagnostic features. The ELDiP is designed to quickly evaluate data from the detector system as it is downloaded during this early stage of the flight, check for nominal detector and optical behavior, and serve as a preliminary quick-look data reduction and analysis tool for observed spectra. Simulated data using ExoSim2 were used to validate this pipeline (see Figure 20), with a data structure mimicking that generated by instrument’s detector system. The pipeline is designed to be used with observed data but has thus far only been tested with simulated data. The terminology used to describe different aspects of the detector readout is described by Figures 20 and 21.

*Figure 21: A diagram of the readout scheme of EXCITE. Each EXCITE “observation” consists of multiple “groups” of NDRs, which are discrete detector measurements taken without a detector reset. In early stages of data processing, groups may also be referred to as “ramps” due to the build-up of charge on a detector pixel. Once a ramp approaches the full-well depth (the maximum charge a pixel can store before saturation), it is reset, and a new ramp begins after a chosen amount of time. For simplicity, the ramps are drawn as linear.*

The ELDiP operates in several consecutive but independent stages:

Stage 0 consists of data read-in and set-up. This stage is performed on one group of non-destructive reads (NDRs) at a time (i.e., the input will consist of several consecutive NDRs forming one group/ramp). An NDR is a discrete voltage measurement across a window of detector pixels to measure signal accumulation without resetting the stored charge in each pixel. Data is separated into its two separate science channels, and several observing parameters are set: the exposure time of each NDR, detector well depth, gain, and read noise. Stage 0 outputs a separate FITS file for each science channel, which are used in the subsequent pipeline steps.

Stage 1 consists of NDR corrections which do not depend on the observed target. Steps of this stage are performed on the outputs of Stage 0, i.e., FITS files containing groups of NDRs, either from CH1 or CH2. We first perform a saturation correction. Saturated pixels are identified as any pixel exceeding the full well depth (shown in Figure 21). Saturated pixels in the dataset are masked, and their values are not considered in future steps. A check is performed to ensure that any pixel flagged as saturated is also flagged in subsequent NDRs within the group. An optional step also flags the 4 fully bordering pixels of any saturated pixel as also saturated. After this step, we perform a dark current subtraction. We assign each detector pixel a dark current value based on dark exposures performed prior to flight. The dark current pixel map is subtracted from each NDR. Then, we perform a reference pixel correction. Reference pixels are defined as the 4 leftmost columns for CH1 and the 4 rightmost columns for CH2. Here, each “column” spans the spatial direction, and each “row” spans the spectral direction. As shown in Figure 20, the CH1 “fast” readout direction is left-to-right, such that the reference pixels are read out at the beginning of each row. For CH2, fast readout is performed right-to-left, such that the reference pixels in the rightmost column are read out at the beginning of each row. The “slow” readout direction is then vertical: each entire row is read out in the fast scan direction before moving up column-wise in the slow direction. Following Bushouse et al., [13] we use a sliding average method with a tunable box size to determine the reference pixel correction for each row of data. The reference pixel values are subtracted from each row in each NDR.

A nonlinearity correction is performed on the group to account for systematic nonlinearities in the charge accumulation of the detector pixels. Systematic nonlinearities are first characterized from flat-field images taken prior to science flight. For benchmarking, we used simulated flat-field groups with 5% deviations from linear to test the functionality of this step in the pipeline. We characterize the detector pixel nonlinearity and apply the correction to our data based on the method described by Hilbert. [27] Finally, we identify and mask out pixels containing data jumps between consecutive NDRs, such as cosmic rays and dark pixels. The algorithm used to define a data jump is based on the algorithm described by Anderson and Gordon. [2] This step of the pipeline iterates over the algorithm, identifying and flagging outlier pixels until no more jumps are detected.

Stage 2 performs corrections which are dependent on the location of the target spectrum on the detector. Within each NDR, we first place a large rectangular aperture around the entire spectral trace of the observed target. To identify the spectral boundaries of the aperture, we take column-wise medians of the NDR and difference adjacent column medians to locate jumps at the start and end of the spectral trace. To identify the aperture’s spatial boundaries, we take row-wise medians of the NDR and fit a Gaussian to the row medians to locate the central pixel of the target PSF. The spatial boundaries are then defined as the nearest integer number of pixels that encompasses the FWHM of the PSF.

After the rectangular target aperture is established, the background is subtracted to remove $1/f$ noise. We define rectangular background apertures as a default 20 pixels away from the edges of the detector in all directions and 20 pixels spatially separated from the defined target aperture. The background values are defined as the median value in each column within the background apertures, and a column-wise background subtraction is performed over the entire NDR. Locations of target and background apertures are shown in Figure 20.

For an instrument performance check, the target trace is then split up into spectral bins given the spectral resolution of the spectrograph. The same method of finding the spatial aperture boundaries is then applied to each spectral bin, allowing the spatial aperture size to vary over wavelength depending on the width of the PSF. At each spectral bin, the target trace centroid, width, and symmetry versus wavelength is plotted to ensure the trace is optimally positioned on the detector and that optical performance is nominal. If this stage identifies variations in PSF shape or large changes in the position of the spectral trace, optical alignment can be checked and motors can be tuned while the instrument is within line-of-sight.

After all NDR-level corrections have been performed, a ramp-fitting step determines the mean count rate for each pixel within each group. This step performs a linear fit to each pixel ramp (nonlinearity corrects have already been applied), with custom treatment to avoid masked pixels–data jumps or saturated pixels–within the group. At the end of Stage 2, all NDR-level and group-level corrections have been performed. Each group is represented by one count rate (flux) value for further time-series analysis.

Stage 3 creates a time series of the resulting flux values after Stages 0–2 have been performed on each group. Stage 3 creates a singular image using the time-median flux in order to check the target spectrum. The spectral bins defined in Stage 2 are used to create a spectrum of the target, which is compared against a spectral model to monitor data quality. The ELDiP is programmed to compare the observed spectrum against a blackbody spectrum of the target’s temperature, but can receive more specific input spectral models. This stage also produces white light curves for each of the science channels. During the line-of-sight portion of the flight, we do not expect to observe transits. In the case we do, Stage 3 has an optional step to fit white light curves to batman [35] transit models. All further data reduction and analysis will be performed by more specialized pipelines.

When the ELDiP is run front-to-back, it has an option to produce plots for visual checks of each correction step. It will automatically save a flag for 1) temporal or spectral variations of the trace centroid location; 2) PSF asymmetries; and 3) large differences in observed versus model spectra. In doing so, the pipeline is designed to identify issues that are correctable either at the detector stage, with the pointing system, or in the optical alignment early in the flight and before any science targets are observed.

## V Integration and Testing and Flight Campaigns

In preparation for the flight campaigns, the EXCITE payload was tested extensively at the subsystem level. This included 1) initial on-sky performance verification of the gondola pointing system at StarSpec Technologies; 2) as-delivered telescope alignment verification; 3) the first complete telescope and gondola assembly at Brown University; 4) telescope alignment and on-sky pointing verification at CSBF in Palestine, Texas; 5) thermal vacuum (TVAC) testing of the gimbal motors and flight computers at CSBF in Palestine, Texas; 6) TVAC testing of the cryostat, fluid loop, and WCS controllers at NASA Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC); and 7) extensive testing of the complete EXCITE instrument before flight at CSBF in Fort Sumner, New Mexico. Section V.1 outlines the integration procedure of the EXCITE payload after component-level testing. Section V.2 describes the results from the 2023 Fort Sumner campaign. Section V.3 discusses the performance of EXCITE during its engineering flight from the 2024 Fort Sumner campaign. The purpose of the engineering flight was to validate instrument operation before an LDB mission from the Antarctic. Much of the gondola/ACS has flight heritage, but we demonstrated the complete science instrument for the first time from a balloon platform. Section V.4 details the refurbishments and improvements made to the payload since the engineering flight, in preparation for an Antarctic LDB flight.

### V.1 Payload Integration

After lab and TVAC testing to verify component-level functionality, we prepare the payload for flight using the following top-level integration procedure:

- 1. Install the ACADIA inside the cryostat;

- 2. Install the spectrograph inside the cryostat;

- 3. Install the detector inside the cryostat;

- 4. Close cryostat and verify detector system operation;

- 5. Integrate telescope with inner frame;

- 6. Align the primary and secondary telescope mirrors using a Takahashi collimating scope;

- 7. Align a collimated beam source to the telescope primary mirror input (a so-called artificial star);

- 8. Using the artificial star, align the visible light telescope beam with FGC by adjusting the angle of the tip-tilt mirror mount;

- 9. Integrate the cryogenic receiver with the telescope and inner frame;

- 10. Using the artificial star and the FSVC, align the infrared telescope beam with the entrance field stop of the spectrograph by adjusting tip-tilt on D1;

- 11. Mount the middle frame inside the outer frame of the gondola;

- 12. Integrate the science instrument with the gondola by mounting the inner frame on the middle frame;

- 13. Put on the gondola hat by attaching to the outer frame;

- 14. Cool the cryostat and tune the cryogenic system’s vibration reduction system;

- 15. Complete integrated system tests, including on-sky optical and pointing verification tests;

- 16. Integrate payload with CSBF instrument package and verify compatibility between the two systems.

Once compatibility with CSBF hardware is confirmed, the payload may be declared flight-ready.

### V.2 2023 Fort Sumner Campaign

The 2023 balloon campaign was EXCITE’s first comprehensive I&T campaign. We declared flight readiness in early September, but were unable to launch due to poor weather and operational priorities over the next month. Nonetheless, this campaign included extensive ground testing and many nights of on-sky operations. We verified successful ground operation of the whole instrument, as well as compatibility with CSBF hardware.

EXCITE performed its first fully-integrated on-sky pointing tests during the 2023 campaign, including 3-axes pointing with tracking on both star cameras. Figure 6 shows the EXCITE payload during an on-sky pointing test from the highbay in Fort Sumner. We showed seeing-limited ground pointing down to 1–3 ′′ (1- $\sigma$ ). During one ground-pointing session, the boresight star camera stabilized with 1- $\sigma$ pointing of 2.63 ′′ and 1.67 ′′ in the cross-elevation and elevation directions, respectively. The cross-elevation direction is orthogonal to the elevation axis. With the entire instrument operational, the ACS performed nominally. Moving parts from the cryogenic system did not measurably impact pointing performance. Based on the pointing stability of the EXCITE payload during ground-pointing and comparing with the in-flight performance of the SuperBIT experiment, we expect gondola stability at the 0.2–0.3 ′′ (1- $\sigma$ ) level for EXCITE.

In addition to stabilizing the gondola, we also tested the FGS on-sky. Figure 22 shows the performance of the FGS during a 2023 on-sky pointing test from the ground. Atmospheric seeing limited the FGS stabilization to the 0.1 ′′ (1- $\sigma$ ) level and moved the PSF on the FGC considerably from frame to frame. Nevertheless, the FGS gain parameters were tuned for the highbay environment, which allowed the FGS to stabilize at a level that is indicative of sub-arcsecond performance during flight. The gyroscope-limited performance at the FGS was at the 0.02–0.08 ′′ (1- $\sigma$ ) level. Gyroscope-limited pointing occurs when the ACS preferentially weights the inertial measurements from the gyroscopes over optical centroiding with the FGS and star cameras, which quickly becomes seeing-limited on the ground. When the payload is at float altitudes and is not seeing-limited, the 1- $\sigma$ on-sky stability with star cameras is expected to become more aligned with the demonstrated gyroscope-limited pointing. A complete discussion of the EXCITE gondola pointing performance during the 2023 campaign is provided by Romualdez et al. [56]

The rest of the science instrument worked as expected. The cryogenic system maintained the required internal temperatures. We enabled the cryocooler vibration reduction system for the first time on the integrated instrument, verifying the functionality and performance of the active and passive vibration reduction modes over a range of operating conditions. [30] Science detector operation was verified, and we used the FSVC for the first time.

### V.3 2024 Fort Sumner Flight

EXCITE’s 2024 I&T campaign was largely uneventful, with just 17 days between payload arrival and flight readiness. Similar to the 2023 campaign, we demonstrated the seeing-limited ground pointing at the 1–2 ′′ level using the star cameras. Likewise, with the FGS enabled, the stars on the FGC showed the same seeing-limited obfuscation down to 0.1 ′′. The FSVC readout was streamlined and made for easier image capturing. This allowed us to more effectively aim the science beam onto the input field stop. Figure 23 shows an image from the FSVC with a focused beam directed onto the field stop of the spectrograph during a pre-flight on-sky pointing test.

EXCITE launched from Fort Sumner on August 31, 2024, at 07:22:00 local time (MDT/GMT-6:00). A photo of EXCITE on the flight line before launch is shown in Figure 24. The flight ended at 17:35:31 MDT and lasted for 10 hours, 13 minutes, and 31 seconds. A plot of the GPS altitude data is shown in Figure 25. EXCITE reached a mean float altitude of 39.75 km at around 10:30 MDT. EXCITE had about 5 hours at float altitudes, making a few rapid 0.25 km oscillations during the first two hours at float before slowing down and oscillating 0.5 km over the remaining 3 hours. The payload did not see any significant drop in altitude during data acquisition, and even reached altitudes > 40 km about a half hour before termination. We mounted a 360∘ camera to the bow of the gondola, and Figure 26 shows a cropped image taken by this camera during the flight. EXCITE traveled $\sim$ 650 km west of Fort Sumner and landed in the Fort Apache Reservation near Show Low, Arizona. The payload was recovered successfully with no significant damage incurred during flight, termination, or landing. Section V.3.1 reports the performance of the gondola and ACS. #### V.3.1 Gondola & ACS Flight Performance

During flight, the gondola and ACS largely performed as expected. We were able to stabilize the gondola to < 1 ′′ during the flight. EXCITE demonstrated sub-arcsecond telescope stabilization over 15-minute periods when the payload was stabilizing with the 3-axes gimbal motors. This is an example of gyroscope-limited pointing defined in Section V.2. EXCITE stabilized at a gimbal position of 55.1∘ elevation, 0∘ roll, and $\sim$ 180∘ anti-Sun in azimuth and demonstrated 0.829 ′′ (1- $\sigma$ ) stability measured by the gyroscopes.

Unfortunately, the payload lost communication with the Trimble GPS compass immediately after launch, resulting in a loss of absolute azimuth information during the entire flight. This hindered our ability to track on pre-assigned sky targets, which we selected for their brightness and observational stability (both photometrically stable and viewable for for hours at a time within EXCITE’s pointing constraints.) As a result, on-sky tracking of stars on the boresight and roll cameras lasted for only a few minutes before stars left our field, which was not enough time to enable the FGS and direct the beam into the spectrograph.

*Figure 26: A photo of EXCITE at float altitudes captured by a 360∘ camera mounted to the front of the payload. The photo does not show the full 360∘ perspective. The radiator panels are seen at the bottom of the photo, and the parachute can be seen in orange at the top of the photo. An enclosure for the fluid loop pumps and tubing can be seen in the top left.*

In addition, the angular travel of the elevation axis was limited to $\sim$ 45∘–57∘, instead of the nominal 22∘–57∘. This contributed to the relatively short amount of time where we were tracking on random sky targets. This would not have limited our ability to track on pre-assigned targets, which were selected to peak in the upper range of the telescope’s elevation travel. We believe this problem was caused by a CTE mismatch between the frameless motor bearing housings (aluminum) and the bearings themselves (stainless steel). They were a press fit at room temperature; we believe that when the payload cooled during ascent through the troposphere, the housings contracted enough to plastically deform the bearings. We discuss re-engineering and testing of this system following the 2024 flight in Section V.4.

#### V.3.2 Science Instrument Flight Performance

While the problems with the ACS described above prevented us from measuring a stellar spectrum, the science instrument otherwise performed nominally in flight. We tested many operating modes of the detector system, from windowed readout of spectral channels to full frame images at maximum bandwidth. We tested all mechanisms and actuators that are integral to the science instrument, including focus and tip/tilt of both the FGS and the telescope secondary mirror. If we had been able to lock on a target with the FGS, we are confident that the spectrometer would have performed the same in flight as on the ground.

The cryogenic system was functional during the entire flight and met EXCITE’s thermal requirements. We intentionally opted out of closed loop temperature control for the majority of flight, instead opting to explore the operational ranges of the cryocoolers to determine allowable margin and system behavior at different input powers. Figure 27 shows the power drawn by the cryocoolers over the duration of the flight. The percent of maximum allowable drive power is also shown to highlight that the cryocoolers could have been driven to higher cooling powers. The temperatures during flight of the cold components inside the cryogenic receiver are shown in Figure 28. Figure 29 shows the temperatures of the warm components: the cryocooler skins, radiator panels, fluid pumps, and methanol reservoirs. The shapes of the temperature profiles in Figures 28 and 29 can be correlated to the changes in input power to the cryocoolers; the cryogenic temperatures will decrease when the input power increases, and the cryocooler skin temperatures will increase when the input power increases.

To avoid overheating the cryocooler skins while on the launch pad, the cryocoolers were not driven to their nominal operating power, and the temperatures of the optics shell and the ACADIA began the flight at 143 K. The 100 K stage continued to cool during the flight, and once we determined that the skin temperatures were stable and adjusted to the ambient temperature at float, we increased the input power to the 100 K cryocooler to 180 W. The ACADIA was PID-controlled at 127 K during the last stage of the flight, and achieved a 1- $\sigma$ temperature stability of 0.01 K for 30 minutes. By the end of the flight, the 100 K cold tip had cooled to 100.9 K, drawing $\sim$ 190 W. The optics shell temperature cooled to as low as 125.0 K at less than 90% of maximum operating power.

The detector stayed below 57.5 K during the entire flight once it reached float. Its cryocooler drew on average about 110 W, about 50–60% of its maximum drive power. At the temperatures measured during flight, the dark current on the H2RG is negligible for EXCITE.

The cryocooler control electronics’ vibration-reduction systems functioned nominally during the flight. Exported vibration levels measured by the accelerometers in flight were comparable to those we measured on the ground, and we measured no negative effects to the pointing system due to vibrations from the cryocooler compressors.

The heat dissipation scheme for the cryocoolers also worked well. The cryocooler skin temperatures remained slightly above ambient for the entire flight, well within their safe operating range. The bulb of the 100 K cryocooler, the warmest component between the two cryocoolers, reached 27 ∘C at its largest input power during the flight. The radiator panels stayed below 0 ∘C. The radiator panels showed no signs of azimuthal dependency as the payload faced towards the Sun during points of the flight. Even as we increased the input power to the cryocoolers, the radiator panels maintained stable temperatures. The fluid pumps warmed to between $\sim$ 25–28 ∘C, well within their operational temperature limits, and operated normally for the entire flight.

### V.4 Refurbishments

To prepare for a long-duration science flight, we have made several refurbishments and upgrades to EXCITE. Motivated by the loss of the GPS compass, for future flights we plan to utilize pinhole sun sensors to provide redundant azimuth determination. If the GPS compass were to fail again, we can use the sun sensors to orient the azimuth of the payload to < 0.5∘ accuracy, and feed that information back to the magnetometer and assist the star cameras in solving the payload’s absolute attitude. The sun sensor design is based on the ones flown on the BLASTPol [21] and EBEX [1] missions. Following the design by Korotkov et al.,[33] the sun sensor operates as a pinhole camera, projecting the Sun’s image through a 200 µm diameter circular aperture onto a 9 mm $\times$ 9 mm position-sensitive detector (PSD). By detecting the image position, the sensor determines its orientation relative to the Sun. With a 40∘ field of view and fixed mounting on the gondola, it provides azimuth and elevation angles of the Sun relative to the payload. EXCITE will operate three sun sensors. These units have been tested at the component level and will be integrated with the payload before the science flight. We calibrated the sun sensors by tracking the position of the Sun at an altitude of about 25 m, and they have demonstrated an accuracy of 0.24∘ rms in measuring the Sun’s position in both elevation and azimuth. This results in an accuracy of 0.35∘ rms in measuring the absolute position of the Sun.

To remedy the CTE mismatch in the frameless motors, we remachined the bearing housings from steel. We then tested the elevations drives under representative loading over a wide range of operating conditions. To achieve the correct loading, we fabricated a “mock inner frame,” composed of the frameless motors, the coarse elevation stepper motors, and 225 kg of steel and aluminum sandwiched between the two sets of motors in order to simulate the mass of the science instrument. We then tested the assembly in a TVAC chamber at CSBF in Palestine, Texas. In this test, the mock inner frame was actuated through the full elevation range at pressures spanning 4–800 mbar and at ambient temperatures between -60 ∘C and 40 ∘C, including a cold soak at -60 ∘C for 1 hour. The elevation motors operated as expected at all pressures and temperatures during a simulated ascent through the troposphere.

Additionally, we cleaned the primary and secondary mirrors to remove any contaminants that accumulated on their surfaces during flight and after landing. After subsequent re-alignment of the telescope optics, we are continuing to perform full system tests, such as on-sky pointing and thermal cycling the cryogenic system. We constructed an artificial source in order to enable the ACS in the case of poor outdoor seeing, and we anticipate it will aid us in aligning the telescope beam onto the detector focal plane. To reduce electromagnetic interference (EMI), we rebuilt our cryocooler power supplies to include EMI filters. We also integrated the solar panel arrays, which EXCITE will fly during an LDB flight.

## VI Summary and Outlook

Characterizing exoplanet atmospheres is a rapidly growing field. The methods and simulation efforts to quantify chemical composition, heat dynamics, and energy recirculation on highly-irradiated hot Jupiters are well-known and practiced. Despite these efforts, the amount of observational data to constrain this large parameter space is lacking. White light phase curves of hot Jupiters are abundant, but do not probe the three-dimensional structure of the exoplanet atmosphere. Similarly, measurements that are taken during only transit and only through secondary eclipse are limited since they do not spatially resolve the exoplanet atmosphere, can suffer from degeneracies when disentangling chemical abundances from thermal emission, measure only the limb of the atmosphere (for transits), and provide only hemispherical averages (for secondary eclipses). Full-orbit spectroscopic phase curves solve these problems, but they are challenging and resource-intensive observations to make. Only a handful of spectroscopic phase curves exist, and all require shared space-based observatories. EXCITE will be the first instrument dedicated to making these observations, with the capability to double to the number of spectroscopic phase curves that exist. In the process, EXCITE will be the first instrument verify the observational and systematic detrending techniques required to obtain phase-resolved spectra from a balloon platform.

We report the mechanical, optical, and thermal design for the EXCITE payload, as well as results from radiometric simulations, jitter simulations, spectral image generation, and data reduction tools. We show that EXCITE is expected to be photon-noise limited by the target across the majority of the passband, and we expect jitter noise to be subdominant to Earth’s atmosphere and thermal emission. We understand the systematic environment from a correlated and uncorrelated noise perspective, and we show that EXCITE can meet its pointing and thermal requirements with margin from a balloon environment. EXCITE flew an engineering flight from Fort Sumner, New Mexico in August 2024. The gondola and ACS delivered sub-arcsecond stability. We could not track stars for hours-long due to a loss in GPS compass, but the star cameras were able to track stars for $\sim$ 30 minute durations. The cryogenic system met all thermal requirements with significant margin on the input power to the cryocoolers. The cryostat cooled the detector to 55 K and the optics shell to 125 K, and the heat rejection scheme worked well. The detector system and all onboard electronics performed nominally. We have since made refurbishments and upgrades to the payload to fix the problems encountered during flight.

We are currently preparing for an LDB flight in the 2026-2027 Austral Summer. EXCITE will deliver high-quality spectroscopic phase curves and significantly increase the available spectroscopic observational data on hot Jupiters. EXCITE aims to set the standard for phase curve observing and exoplanet atmosphere characterization from a balloon platform.

## Abstract

The Super-Pressure Balloon-borne Imaging Telescope (SuperBIT) completed its science flight in April 2023, obtaining imaging data for 30 galaxy clusters. In this work, we present the first weak-lensing convergence maps from these observations, using six clusters selected from the 30 targets. We construct background-galaxy catalogs using SuperBIT’s three-band photometry and a color–color-based method to separate foreground and background galaxies, and use the calibrated galaxy shapes presented in Lensing in the Blue III to reconstruct the weak-lensing convergence field using the Kaiser–Squires inversion. We compare the convergence signal-to-noise maps for the six clusters with independent tracers, including X-ray emission and red-sequence cluster-member number-density maps. These results demonstrate the first successful weak-lensing mass mapping with imaging from a sub-orbital astronomical observatory.

]

## I Introduction

Galaxy clusters are among the largest gravitationally bound structures in the Universe and are therefore one of the most powerful probes of cosmic evolution. The abundance of galaxy clusters as a function of their mass and redshift can provide independent constraints on several cosmological parameters, including the dark energy equation of state, the amplitude of matter-density fluctuations $\sigma_{8}$ , and the sum of neutrino masses $\sum m_{\nu}$ [83, 2, 47, 49]. Targeted observations of merging cluster systems can also be used to place constraints on alternative dark-matter models [22, 63, 74].

One of the most direct ways to probe the total mass distribution of galaxy clusters is through the gravitational-lensing signatures imprinted on background galaxies. Strong gravitational lenses produce prominent distortions such as arcs and multiple images of background galaxies [56, and references therein]. The weak-lensing counterpart produces much smaller, typically sub-percent-level distortions in the two-dimensional light profiles of background galaxies [11]. Since its first detections [88, 7, 43, 78], weak gravitational lensing has become one of the most powerful observational probes to study the dark sector of the Universe.

The reconstruction of weak-lensing signal requires imaging of exceptional quality and meticulous processing to construct accurate catalogs of background galaxy shapes. In the last few decades, many space- and ground-based observatories have successfully measured weak-lensing signals, each with their own advantages and limitations. Ground-based telescopes benefit from the ability to obtain long integration times, allowing them to accumulate sufficient signal from very faint galaxies. However, the unpredictable and spatially varying atmosphere makes it challenging to model the point spread function (PSF) and to accurately resolve and measure the shapes of faint galaxies. Space-based telescopes, on the other hand, provide diffraction-limited imaging but typically have smaller fields of view and require substantially greater resources and costs for deployment and operation.

The Super-Pressure Balloon-borne Imaging Telescope (SuperBIT) was designed to combine some of the advantages of ground- and space-based observations [65, 64, 31]. During its nearly 45-night science flight in April 2023 [61, 51], SuperBIT achieved near-diffraction-limited image quality at an altitude of approximately 33 km above sea level, placing it above more than $99\%$ of the Earth’s atmosphere. With near-space-like observing conditions, the mission was accomplished at a cost of approximately $10^{-3}$ that of a comparable space-based mission.

This paper is part of the Lensing in the Blue (LITB) series within the SuperBIT collaboration. Paper I [70] and Paper II [52, hereafter LITB II] forecasted the expected weak-lensing efficiency of blue-band observations, while Paper III [66, hereafter LITB III] presented the processing and calibration of the post-flight SuperBIT imaging data. This paper, Paper IV, presents weak-lensing convergence maps for six of the 30 cluster fields processed in 66, selected based on the strength of their reconstructed weak-lensing signal. We compare the resulting weak-lensing signal with independent tracers of the clusters’ baryonic matter, including X-ray emission and red-sequence cluster-member galaxies. To the best of our knowledge, this work presents the first weak-lensing signal reconstruction obtained from the stratosphere, demonstrating the potential of balloon-based observatories as a more economical, and to some degree serviceable alternative to fully space-based missions for future weak-lensing and astrophysical surveys.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section II, we provide a brief overview of the data, including the calibrated galaxy shapes and photometry. In Section III, we describe the methods used in this work, including foreground–background sample separation, our cluster-member identification scheme, and mass mapping technique. In Section IV, we present the weak-lensing convergence maps for our cluster sample, together with comparisons to independent probes such as X-ray emission and the spatial distribution of red-sequence cluster members. Finally, in Section V, we summarize our results and discuss future prospects.

## II Data

The imaging data obtained during the SuperBIT 2023 science flight have been processed through a dedicated weak-lensing analysis pipeline, resulting in shape catalogs for the detected sources. A detailed description of the data reduction, shape-measurement pipeline, and an extensive suite of systematic tests is presented in 66. Here, we provide a brief overview of the final data products relevant to the construction of the weak-lensing convergence maps.

### II.1 Shape Measurement

We parameterize the shape of each detected galaxy using the two-component complex ellipticity:

$$ \mathbb{e}=e_{1}+ie_{2},\qquad e_{1}=e\cos(2\beta),\quad e_{2}=e\sin(2\beta), $$

where $\beta$ is the angle between the x-axis and the major axis. The scalar ellipticity amplitude $e$ is defined as:

$$ e=\frac{a-b}{a+b}, $$

with $a$ and $b$ denoting the semi-major and semi-minor axes, respectively, of the isophotes of the intrinsic, pre-PSF galaxy light profile.

We infer the pre-PSF galaxy parameters using a Bayesian forward-modeling framework implemented with ngmix [72, 73]. To correct for observational non-idealities that would otherwise bias the weak-lensing reconstruction, we subsequently calibrate the galaxy shapes using Metacalibration [39, 71]. In this approach, small artificial shears are applied to each galaxy image, and the resulting change in the measured ellipticity is used to estimate its shear response. To first order in the applied shear $\mathbf{\gamma}$ ,

$$ \mathbf{e}(\mathbf{\gamma})\simeq\mathbf{e}(0)+\mathbf{R}\mathbf{\gamma}, $$

where $\mathbf{e}(0)$ denotes the ellipticity measured in the absence of an applied shear and

$$ R_{ij}=\left.\frac{\partial e_{i}}{\partial\gamma_{j}}\right|_{\mathbf{\gamma}=0} $$

is the Metacalibration shear response matrix. The ensemble-averaged response is measured from the full galaxy sample and used to calibrate the measured ellipticities. The resulting calibrated shapes can then be spatially averaged to estimate the weak-lensing shear field.

For the full SuperBIT 2023 data set, the mean source density after the fiducial selection is $n_{\rm sel}=13.38~\mathrm{arcmin}^{-2}$ , with an effective source density [38] of $n_{\rm eff}=10.66~\mathrm{arcmin}^{-2}$ . These values, however, vary substantially across individual targets as a result of differences in exposure depth, observing conditions, and image quality (see Table 2 of 66). We therefore choose the spatial resolution of the weak-lensing maps, as well as the smoothing kernel size, on a target-by-target basis, taking into account the available source density and the quality of the imaging data.

### II.2 Photometry

*Figure 1: Foreground–background classification in the SuperBIT pipeline. Left: An example of the trained pixel mask in the $(u-b)$ versus $(b-g)$ color–color space for a cluster at redshift $z_{\rm cluster}=0.24$ . Right: Validation of the pixel-mask classifier using independent photometric redshifts from the COSMOS2020 data. The background contamination (top) and retained background-source fraction (bottom) are shown as a function of cluster redshift for three choices of the hyperparameters $(\tau,\eta)$ : aggressive (red), balanced (blue), and relaxed (green).*

Taking advantage of the high transmission and low sky background at blue wavelengths, most of the SuperBIT 2023 imaging data were obtained in three filters at the blue end of the optical spectrum: F400W ( $u$ ), F480W ( $b$ ), and F600W ( $g$ ). The transmission curves of these filters are presented in Figure 2 of 52. We use F480W ( $b$ ) as the detection band and perform forced photometry in F400W ( $u$ ) and F600W ( $g$ ) at the positions of all objects detected in F480W. We then calibrate the measured fluxes using the AB-magnitude zero points derived in 66.

We correct our galaxy photometry for Galactic dust extinction using the model of [35], which provides wavelength-dependent dust extinction curves $A(\lambda)/A(V)$ parameterized by $R(V)$ , the ratio of total-to-selective extinction:

$$ R(V)=\frac{A(V)}{E(B-V)}. $$

We adopt $R(V)=3.1$ , a commonly used value representative of diffuse Milky Way dust [41]. For each SuperBIT band, we calculate the band-averaged extinction relative to $A(V)$ , weighted by the filter transmission:

$$ \frac{A_{\rm band}}{A_{V}}=\frac{\displaystyle\int S_{\rm band}(\lambda)\frac{A_{\lambda}}{A_{V}}\lambda\mathrm{d}\lambda}{\displaystyle\int S_{\rm band}(\lambda)\lambda\mathrm{d}\lambda}, $$

where $S_{\rm band}(\lambda)$ denotes the transmission of the corresponding SuperBIT filter. We use the dustmaps software [36] to query the CSFD Galactic dust reddening map [19] at the sky position of each galaxy, calculate the appropriate $A_{\rm band}$ in each filter from Equation 6, and finally apply the corresponding extinction correction to the galaxies’ measured magnitudes.

## III Methods

### III.1 Foreground–Background Separation

In addition to precise shape measurements, reliable reconstruction of weak-lensing signal requires robust separation of background source galaxies from foreground galaxies. Background source selection is often performed using photometric redshifts, whose accuracy depends on having a sufficient number of independent photometric bands spanning a broad wavelength range to break degeneracies between a galaxy’s spectral energy distribution (SED) and its redshift. However, even surveys with four to six broad photometric bands can suffer a 20–30% catastrophic outlier fraction, driven by color–redshift degeneracies that persist when the available bands do not sufficiently extend into the ultraviolet or infrared [54]. This limitation is particularly acute for SuperBIT, whose three bands, F400W ( $u$ ), F480W ( $b$ ), and F600W ( $g$ ), occupy a relatively narrow blue-optical wavelength range and overlap substantially in wavelength (Figure 2 of 52). Consequently, they provide limited independent information about a galaxy’s SED, making photometric redshift estimates highly uncertain. Instead, we adopt a color–color (CC)-based selection scheme that uses the two independent colors available from the three SuperBIT bands: $(u-b)$ and $(b-g)$ .

To identify weak-lensing source galaxies, we developed a novel pixel-based classifier in the $(u-b)$ versus $(b-g)$ color–color space. This two-dimensional color space is first divided into a regular grid of “meta-pixels”, as demonstrated in the left panel of Figure 1. The pixel-based classifier is then trained using the $(u-b)$ and $(b-g)$ colors of all SuperBIT galaxies with existing external spectroscopic redshift measurements (hereafter, training objects). These external spectroscopic redshifts are obtained primarily from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) DR1 [1] and the NASA/IPAC Extragalactic Database (NED)11 1 https://ned.ipac.caltech.edu/ [55]. In total, $4278$ external spectroscopic redshifts are available and used in our pipeline. For a cluster at redshift $z_{\rm cluster}$ , each training object is labeled as foreground $(z\leq z_{\rm cluster})$ or background $(z>z_{\rm cluster})$ . Each meta-pixel is then assigned a foreground purity, defined as the fraction of training objects within that pixel that have $(z\leq z_{\rm cluster})$ , weighted by the inverse of their mean color variance. A pixel is flagged as foreground-dominated for a given $z_{\rm cluster}$ when its foreground purity exceeds a threshold $\tau$ , provided that it also contains at least $\eta$ training objects; the parameters $\tau$ and $\eta$ serve as the tunable hyperparameters of the classifier. An example of the resulting foreground mask for a cluster at $z_{\rm cluster}=0.24$ is shown in the left panel of Figure 1. Of the 352 pixels identified as foreground-dominated by the purity criterion, 88 also satisfy the minimum occupancy requirement and therefore constitute the final mask.

Once trained, the pixel mask is applied to SuperBIT galaxies without external redshift measurements. Based on their measured colors, objects falling within a foreground-dominated pixel are classified as foreground galaxies, while objects outside the mask are retained as background candidates.

Left: Color–magnitude diagram showing $b-g$ color (derived from SuperBIT F480W and F600W magnitudes) versus F480W ( $b$ )-band magnitude. Grey points denote all galaxies in the field of view; magenta points mark spectroscopically confirmed cluster members. We validate the classifier using two SuperBIT pointings in the Cosmic Evolution Survey (COSMOS) field [69], COSMOSk and COSMOS113, for which accurate photometric redshifts are available from the COSMOS2020 catalog [86]. The validation results are shown in the right panel of Figure 1 for several choices of the hyperparameters $(\tau,\eta)$ . We evaluate the classifier’s performance using two complementary metrics: the background contamination, defined as the fraction of foreground sources remaining in the retained background sample (upper-right panel), and the background completeness, defined as the fraction of background sources retained after the foreground selection (lower-right panel). We explore a range of hyperparameter choices that trade off contamination against completeness. An aggressive configuration, $(\tau,\eta)=(0.5,1)$ , prioritizes low background contamination but removes a larger fraction of genuine background sources. Conversely, a more relaxed configuration, $(\tau,\eta)=(0.9,10)$ , prioritizes background completeness at the expense of increased foreground contamination. For the results shown in this work, we adopt an intermediate configuration $(\tau,\eta)=(0.7,10)$ , which provides a balanced compromise between background completeness and contamination.

### III.2 Cluster-Member Identification

Cluster member galaxies provide an important tracer of the baryonic matter distribution within galaxy clusters and share several physical properties that can be exploited for their identification. Galaxies residing in clusters tend to host older stellar populations and generally have lower star-formation rates than galaxies in the field [25]. In addition, the buildup of metals through multiple generations of star formation produces a prominent feature in the galaxies’ SEDs, known as the 4000 Å break [10]. These features give rise to the well-known red sequence in galaxy color–magnitude diagrams.

The basic procedure of our red-sequence identification algorithm is illustrated in Figure 2. In the left panel, we show the color–magnitude diagram for galaxies in the field of Abell 1689 ( $z_{\rm cluster}=0.1832$ ). The red points indicate confirmed cluster members, identified as galaxies with external spectroscopic redshifts satisfying $|z-z_{\rm cluster}|<0.02$ . We use these confirmed members to determine the location of the red sequence. We first fit a linear relation to their color–magnitude distribution, iteratively removing outliers through sigma clipping. The fit is flux-weighted, giving higher weight to brighter cluster members with more precise photometric measurements. We then define a red-sequence selection region by allowing a color width of 0.1 mag on either side of the best-fitting relation. We additionally impose a faint-end magnitude cut at $\mathrm{mag}_{b}=23$ . Galaxies falling within this red-sequence region and satisfying the magnitude cut are identified as candidate cluster members. We then examine their spatial distribution in sky coordinates, as illustrated in the right panel of Figure 2. Based on the color scatter of the known member galaxies, we find that F480W–F600W ( $b-g$ ) provides the smallest scatter among the color combinations considered and therefore adopt this color for red sequence identification. The resulting cluster-member distributions are compared with the clusters’ weak-lensing signal in Section IV. Our cluster member galaxy identification scheme is described in further detail in Ohashi et al. (in preparation).

### III.3 Mass mapping

We reconstruct convergence maps from the calibrated galaxy shapes of background galaxies described in Section II.1, following the foreground–background separation described in Section III.1, using Kaiser–Squires inversion [42, hereafter KS93]. The convergence $\kappa$ , which describes the isotropic magnification component of the lensing distortion, can be expressed as the ratio of the projected surface mass density $\Sigma$ to the critical surface density $\Sigma_{\rm crit}$ for the lens–source system:

$$ \kappa=\frac{\Sigma}{\Sigma_{\rm crit}},\qquad\Sigma_{\rm crit}=\frac{c^{2}}{4\pi G}\frac{D_{\rm s}}{D_{\rm l}D_{\rm ls}}, $$

where $D_{\rm s}$ , $D_{\rm l}$ , and $D_{\rm ls}$ are the observer–source, observer–lens, and lens–source angular-diameter distances, respectively. The Jacobian of the lens mapping can be expressed in terms of the convergence $\kappa$ and the two components of the complex shear, $\gamma=\gamma_{1}+i\gamma_{2}$ , both of which are linear combinations of the second-order derivatives of the projected lensing potential $\psi$ . Since the intrinsic size distribution of unlensed galaxies is not known, the ensemble-averaged observed galaxy ellipticities provide an estimate of the reduced shear, $g=\gamma/(1-\kappa)$ . In the weak-lensing regime, where $|\kappa|,|\gamma|\ll 1$ , the reduced shear is well approximated by the shear, $g\simeq\gamma$ ; we therefore take the measured reduced shear as an estimator of $\gamma$ in what follows.

Because both $\kappa$ and $\gamma$ are second derivatives of the same lensing potential, a direct relation between them can be derived (KS93; Kaiser 44, Crittenden et al. 23, Umetsu 75) and inverted under the flat-sky approximation [42]. This inversion is usually easier to compute in Fourier space:

$$ \hat{\kappa}(\mathbf{k})=\frac{(k_{1}^{2}-k_{2}^{2})-2ik_{1}k_{2}}{k_{1}^{2}+k_{2}^{2}}\,\hat{\gamma}(\mathbf{k}), $$

where $\hat{\kappa}(\mathbf{k})$ and $\hat{\gamma}(\mathbf{k})$ are the Fourier transforms of $\kappa(\mathbb{\theta})$ and $\gamma(\mathbb{\theta})=\gamma_{1}(\mathbb{\theta})+i\gamma_{2}(\mathbb{\theta})$ , respectively, and $k_{1}$ and $k_{2}$ are the components of the two-dimensional wave vector $\mathbf{k}$ . The real and imaginary parts of the reconstructed convergence correspond to the E- and B-mode components, $\kappa_{\rm E}=\Re(\kappa)$ and $\kappa_{\rm B}=\Im(\kappa)$ , respectively [76, for a review, see]. The E-mode represents the curl-free gravitational lensing signal, whereas the B-mode provides a useful null test for non-lensing contributions, such as residual observational systematics. We therefore use $\kappa_{\rm B}$ as a null test when choosing selection cuts.

In practice, the post-selection-cut background-galaxy shape catalog is binned into two-dimensional meta-pixels. At each pixel, we estimate the shear from an ensemble average of the galaxy shapes, weighted using the inverse-variance weights of 66. Equation 8 is then applied to the resulting shear grid, and the reconstructed maps are smoothed with a Gaussian kernel to suppress shape noise. The meta-pixel size and kernel width ( $\sigma$ ) are chosen separately for each target and listed in Table 1. To quantify the significance of the reconstructed signal, we generate 1000 noise realizations by randomly rotating each galaxy and repeating the mass-mapping procedure. We use the same pixel size and Gaussian smoothing kernel for each realization, and define a signal-to-noise ratio $\mathrm{SNR}=\kappa_{\rm E}/\sigma_{\kappa}$ at each pixel, where $\sigma_{\kappa}$ is the pixel-wise standard deviation across the noise realizations. The $\kappa_{\rm B}$ SNR maps are obtained identically. The full procedure is implemented in the open-source SMPy package [82], which we used for this analysis.

In this section, we present the convergence maps reconstructed from the calibrated shapes of background galaxies. We show the results for six clusters for which we obtain the strongest $\kappa_{\rm E}$ detections. As described in 66, the baseline source-selection cuts adopted in the pipeline were validated using simulations. However, the quality of individual SuperBIT exposures can vary substantially between targets, and consequently the level of residual systematics in the reconstructed convergence maps can also vary. For each target, we therefore perform a grid search around the baseline selection cuts described in 66. We select the combination of cuts that maximizes the $\kappa_{\rm E}$ -mode peak SNR while simultaneously minimizing the $\kappa_{\rm B}$ -mode SNR in the vicinity of the detected $\kappa_{\rm E}$ peak. The selected targets for this work, their redshifts, peak $\kappa_{\rm E}$ SNRs, and the corresponding source-selection cuts are summarized in Table 1. We also report the pixel size and Gaussian smoothing kernel used to construct each convergence map.

Although the SuperBIT 2023 imaging provides a large field of view of approximately $22^{\prime}\times 15.23^{\prime}$ , we do not use the full field for the convergence reconstruction. A roll-stability issue during the observations produced increasingly elliptical PSFs toward the outskirts of the field, resulting in elevated PSF-leakage-related systematics in those regions. We therefore crop the images and restrict the analysis to approximately the central $50\%$ of the field of view, where the image quality is more stable.

Figure 3 shows the reconstructed convergence maps, with the $\kappa_{\rm E}$ signal represented by the blue hue, overlaid with X-ray emission from the Chandra ACIS data, shown in pink. The maps are displayed on top of RGB composite images constructed from the registered SuperBIT coadds in F400W ( $u$ ), F480W ( $b$ ), and F600W ( $g$ ). The corresponding $\kappa_{\rm E}$ and $\kappa_{\rm B}$ SNR maps for each target are presented in Appendix A.

We present the comparison of the red-sequence cluster member galaxy distribution with the reconstructed weak-lensing signal for the six-cluster sample in Figure 4. The background color scale shows the projected density of red-sequence galaxies obtained using the method described in Section III.2, with redder colors representing higher galaxy densities and bluer colors representing underdense regions. Overlaid on the red-sequence density maps are contours of the $\kappa_{\rm E}$ signal-to-noise maps. The darker contours toward the outskirts correspond to lower-SNR, while progressively lighter contours trace the higher-SNR regions toward the peaks. The contours start at SNR = 2 and increase in increments of 1. Comments for individual clusters are presented below.

- • Abell 2384 (N): Abell 2384 is a low-redshift merging cluster system at $z=0.094$ comprised of two unequal mass subclusters in a north-south alignment. The image shown here corresponds to the northern and more massive component, A2384 (N); SuperBIT observations also cover the southern subcluster, A2384 (S). The two subclusters are known to be connected via a large bridge of ICM gas, presumably the signature of a recent interaction [57]; little ongoing star formation in disk galaxies near the cluster core provides further evidence of recent interaction [59]. This cluster is included in the Local Volume Complete Cluster Survey [30].

- • Abell 3411: Part of a merging cluster system with Abell 3412, Abell 3411 (z=0.169) has been well studied in optical, X-ray, sub-millimeter, and radio wavelengths, and has been the subject of multiple previous weak lensing analyses [29, 28]. Radio studies of the Abell 3411–Abell 3412 complex revealed a northern extension [34] and a giant radio halo [81], a feature whose presence generally indicates a recent, massive merger [80]. Abell 3411 is notable because an observed connection between its radio relic and a radio-loud member galaxy helped establish that radio galaxies in galaxy clusters provide seed electrons that can be re-accelerated and revived by merger shocks [79, 90]. While Figures 3–4 only show the central region of Abell 3411, SuperBIT observations also cover its northern extension and its companion Abell 3412.

- • Abell 1689: Abell 1689 is another very well-studied galaxy cluster with a radio relic [77, 24] and pre-existing weak lensing studies. It is among the most massive in the observable Universe, with an estimated mass above $10^{15}M_{\odot}$ [12]. While azimuthally symmetric on the plane of the sky and dynamically relaxed in its appearance, A1689 is significantly elongated along the line of sight, a fact that has been attributed to a merger event at a very small angle from the line of sight [3].

- • Abell S0592: Abell S0592 (also designated SPT-CLJ0638-5358) is a high-mass cluster [12, $\sim 10^{15}M_{\odot}$ ,] at $z=0.23$ whose disturbed ICM [48, 89] with at least one known shock [14] and megaparsec-scale diffuse radio emission [87] suggest that it has recently undergone a major merger. Although Abell S0592 has been observed with the Hubble Space Telescope [27], no gravitational lensing mass maps appear in the literature for it, making ours the first such map for this cluster.

- • 1E 0657-56: Arguably the most famous galaxy cluster in our sample, 1E 0657-56, better known as the Bullet Cluster, has been used as a dark matter laboratory since the pioneering work of [50] and [21]. Its favorable merger geometry along the plane of the sky means that the Bullet Cluster has been the subject of numerous X-ray [18, 68, e.g.,], radio [45, 60, e.g.,], Sunyaev-Zel’dovich effect [9, and references therein] and gravitational lensing studies, with at least three of the latter released in the last 18 months alone [17, 62, 20], and it continues to serve as a benchmark for hydrodynamical simulations of cluster mergers [63, 53, 92].

- • PLCK G287.0+32.9: PLCK G287.0+32.9 is the second-most massive cluster in the Planck sample [58, 46], with many known strong gravitational lenses surrounding the cluster core [91, 26]. Prior weak lensing analyses of this cluster appear in [29] and [28]. Substructures and radio relics, including “megahalo” emission oriented along the merger axis, indicate recent major mergers [8, 13, 67, 60].

## V Conclusion

We present convergence maps for six galaxy clusters selected from the thirty science targets presented in 66. To our knowledge, this work presents the first weak-lensing signal obtained from stratospheric imaging and the first made using blue-band imaging. We also make use of the three-band SuperBIT photometry in F400W ( $u$ ), F480W ( $b$ ), and F600W ( $g$ ) to perform foreground–background galaxy separation, an essential step for weak-lensing analyses, as well as to identify cluster-member galaxies using their location in the color–magnitude diagram.

The cluster targets presented here are selected solely on the strength of their reconstructed $\kappa_{\rm E}$ SNR from Kaiser–Squires inversion. A more detailed investigation of the larger SuperBIT cluster sample is underway (G. Leroy et al., in preparation) and will further develop cluster mass-mapping methods, with particular emphasis on the characterization and mitigation of $\kappa_{\rm B}$ modes, and will explore the physics of the merging clusters. Additional future analyses will investigate the dynamical states of the SuperBIT clusters using Fourier-space coherence measurements [15, 16].

SuperBIT provided an important proof of concept for balloon-borne, near-space astronomical imaging. Beyond weak-lensing studies, its data can enable a range of science investigations, from galaxy evolution to star formation to the distribution of intracluster dust. SuperBIT’s successor mission, GigaBIT [85], is already in development, with a larger mirror, smaller detector pixels, and an improved guidance system designed to provide deeper imaging with enhanced pointing stability. GigaBIT is forecast to achieve a background-source density of approximately 35 galaxies per arcmin2 for a cluster at redshift $z_{\rm cluster}=0.34$ [32]. SuperBIT, and eventually GigaBIT, therefore add a unique capability to NASA’s astronomical data legacy by providing near-space-quality imaging at blue wavelengths.

## Appendix A $\kappa_{\rm B}$ modes

*Figure A1: $\kappa_{\rm E}$ and $\kappa_{\rm B}$ SNR maps for the cluster sample.*

*Figure A2: $\kappa_{\rm E}$ and $\kappa_{\rm B}$ SNR maps for the cluster sample (continued).*

In the weak-lensing regime, gravitational lensing by scalar gravitational potentials produces only curl-free distortions of background galaxy shapes, which contribute to the $\kappa_{\rm E}$ mode. By contrast, a non-zero $\kappa_{\rm B}$ mode can arise from several sources, including residual systematics in the shape-measurement pipeline, masking effects, edge effects, and shape noise. In this section, we assess $\kappa_{\rm B}$ modes for the six clusters discussed in Section IV.

In Figures A1 and A2, we show the $\kappa_{\rm B}$ -mode SNR maps obtained using the final selected galaxy catalog for each cluster field. The maps are constructed using the same pixelization and smoothing parameters listed in Table 1. The definitions of the $\kappa_{\rm E}$ and $\kappa_{\rm B}$ modes, as well as the corresponding SNR estimators, are described in detail in Section III.3. To facilitate visual comparison between the E- and B-mode signals, the color bars of the $\kappa_{\rm E}$ - and $\kappa_{\rm B}$ -mode SNR maps are set to the same range for each cluster. This allows the relative strength of the B-mode signal with respect to the corresponding E-mode signal to be assessed visually. For all targets presented here, we find that the $\kappa_{\rm B}$ modes are generally $\lesssim 3\sigma$ . The exception is A2384 (N), which shows a relatively high $\kappa_{\rm B}$ SNR near the edge of the field of view. A1689 exhibits a $\sim 3.5\sigma$ $\kappa_{\rm B}$ signal near the $\kappa_{\rm E}$ peak; however, the $\kappa_{\rm E}$ SNR reaches $6.87$ . These maps provide visual evidence that the signals observed in Figures 3 and 4 are genuine and unlikely to be significantly affected by residual systematics.
